papers.title: All Languages Matter: On the Multilingual Safety of Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Safety lies at the core of developing and deploying large language models (LLMs). However, previous safety benchmarks only concern the safety in one language, e.g. the majority language in the pretraining data such as English. In this work, we build the first multilingual safety benchmark for LLMs, XSafety, in response to the global deployment of LLMs in practice. XSafety covers 14 kinds of commonly used safety issues across 10 languages that span several language families. We utilize XSafety to empirically study the multilingual safety for 4 widely-used LLMs, including both close-API and open-source models. Experimental results show that all LLMs produce significantly more unsafe responses for non-English queries than English ones, indicating the necessity of developing safety alignment for non-English languages. In addition, we propose several simple and effective prompting methods to improve the multilingual safety of ChatGPT by evoking safety knowledge and improving cross-lingual generalization of safety alignment. Our prompting method can significantly reduce the ratio of unsafe responses from 19.1% to 9.7% for non-English queries. We release our data at https://github.com/Jarviswang94/Multilingual_safety_benchmark.

papers.title: Safety Assessment of Chinese Large Language Models
papers.abstract: With the rapid popularity of large language models such as ChatGPT and GPT-4, a growing amount of attention is paid to their safety concerns. These models may generate insulting and discriminatory content, reflect incorrect social values, and may be used for malicious purposes such as fraud and dissemination of misleading information. Evaluating and enhancing their safety is particularly essential for the wide application of large language models (LLMs). To further promote the safe deployment of LLMs, we develop a Chinese LLM safety assessment benchmark. Our benchmark explores the comprehensive safety performance of LLMs from two perspectives: 8 kinds of typical safety scenarios and 6 types of more challenging instruction attacks. Our benchmark is based on a straightforward process in which it provides the test prompts and evaluates the safety of the generated responses from the evaluated model. In evaluation, we utilize the LLM's strong evaluation ability and develop it as a safety evaluator by prompting. On top of this benchmark, we conduct safety assessments and analyze 15 LLMs including the OpenAI GPT series and other well-known Chinese LLMs, where we observe some interesting findings. For example, we find that instruction attacks are more likely to expose safety issues of all LLMs. Moreover, to promote the development and deployment of safe, responsible, and ethical AI, we publicly release SafetyPrompts including 100k augmented prompts and responses by LLMs.

papers.title: Safety at Scale: A Comprehensive Survey of Large Model and Agent Safety
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of large models, driven by their exceptional abilities in learning and generalization through large-scale pre-training, has reshaped the landscape of Artificial Intelligence (AI). These models are now foundational to a wide range of applications, including conversational AI, recommendation systems, autonomous driving, content generation, medical diagnostics, and scientific discovery. However, their widespread deployment also exposes them to significant safety risks, raising concerns about robustness, reliability, and ethical implications. This survey provides a systematic review of current safety research on large models, covering Vision Foundation Models (VFMs), Large Language Models (LLMs), Vision-Language Pre-training (VLP) models, Vision-Language Models (VLMs), Diffusion Models (DMs), and large-model-powered Agents. Our contributions are summarized as follows: (1) We present a comprehensive taxonomy of safety threats to these models, including adversarial attacks, data poisoning, backdoor attacks, jailbreak and prompt injection attacks, energy-latency attacks, data and model extraction attacks, and emerging agent-specific threats. (2) We review defense strategies proposed for each type of attacks if available and summarize the commonly used datasets and benchmarks for safety research. (3) Building on this, we identify and discuss the open challenges in large model safety, emphasizing the need for comprehensive safety evaluations, scalable and effective defense mechanisms, and sustainable data practices. More importantly, we highlight the necessity of collective efforts from the research community and international collaboration. Our work can serve as a useful reference for researchers and practitioners, fostering the ongoing development of comprehensive defense systems and platforms to safeguard AI models.

papers.title: Enhanced Diagnostic and Interpretable Model for Febrile Diseases Using Explainable AI and Large Language Model
papers.abstract: <p><span>Tropical febrile diseases pose significant public health challenges in tropical regions, particularly in resource-limited settings, where timely and accurate diagnoses are critical for effective disease management. However, existing diagnostic systems are black-box and often lack interpretability, making it difficult for healthcare practitioners to understand and trust machine learning (ML) predictions. Additionally, the existing system excludes younger patients, limiting its applicability. This study aimed to develop an integrated diagnostic system that enhances interpretability by leveraging machine learning (ML), Explainable AI (XAI), and a large language model (LLM). A dataset comprising 3,914 patient records with 32 symptoms was obtained from a New Frontiers in Research Fund-sponsored project and preprocessed for analysis. Random Forest (RF) was trained with hyperparameter tuning using GridSearchCV and evaluated with 5-fold cross-validation to optimize its performance. The tuned model achieved high diagnostic performance, demonstrating its effectiveness in diagnosing six febrile diseases. To enhance interpretability, a Model Interpretability Framework (MIF) was incorporated, integrating Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) for visual insights and ChatGPT for textual explanations. This combination provided users with a clear understanding of the diagnostic process, addressing the limitations of black-box ML models. The system was implemented using Python in a development environment that included Google Colaboratory, Visual Studio Code, Flet, and MySQL for database management. Agile development methodology and Unified Modeling Language tools were employed to create a user-friendly design for clinicians and patients. The diagnostic system was evaluated using precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC metrics. The RF model achieved outstanding precision for most diseases, high recall (≥0.97), and an AUC-ROC of 0.99, indicating nearly flawless training performance with few misclassifications. On the test dataset, the model performed better in diagnosing malaria (F1-score = 88%, precision = 85%), urinary tract infection (F1-score = 72%, precision = 80%), and respiratory tract infection (F1-score = 72%, precision = 77%). The evaluated system demonstrated strong predictive performance, correctly identifying 72 out of 99 tested patient cases, with 26 cases misclassified and one case completely missed. It achieved the highest detection rates for Malaria and HIV/AIDS, accurately identifying all cases without false positives. This work enhances diagnostic solutions for tropical healthcare settings by improving explainability and ensuring inclusivity for younger patients, addressing key limitations in existing systems. The integration of ML, XAI, and LLM enhances diagnostic performance and lays the groundwork for future AI-driven healthcare innovations, ultimately improving health outcomes in resource-scarce regions. Healthcare providers should adopt this system to enhance the efficiency of disease diagnosis and extend the system to diagnose additional medical conditions.&nbsp;</span></p>

literature_themes.theme: Multilingual Safety and Assessment of Large Language Models
literature_themes.summary: This cluster of papers focuses on the safety of large language models (LLMs) across different languages and contexts. It highlights the development of multilingual safety benchmarks, such as XSafety for assessing safety issues in LLMs in multiple languages, and a specific safety assessment for Chinese LLMs. The studies reveal that LLMs tend to produce more unsafe responses for non-English queries and emphasize the need for improved safety measures. Additionally, a comprehensive survey of safety threats and defenses for large models is presented, covering various types of models and their vulnerabilities.
literature_themes.limitations: The studies primarily focus on specific languages (e.g., English and Chinese) and may not fully address the safety concerns in less-represented languages. There is also a need for more extensive evaluation of safety measures across diverse applications and real-world scenarios. The interpretability of models remains a challenge, particularly in medical diagnostics, where trust in AI predictions is crucial.
literature_themes.gap_relevance: This cluster identifies significant gaps in the multilingual safety of LLMs and the need for comprehensive safety assessments across various languages and contexts. It supports research gap identification by highlighting the necessity for improved safety alignment, evaluation frameworks, and interpretability in AI systems, particularly in sensitive applications like healthcare.

literature_themes.theme: Enhancing Few-Shot Recommender Systems with LLMs
literature_themes.summary: This cluster primarily investigates the integration of large language models (LLMs) to improve the performance of few-shot recommender systems. It explores how LLM-enhanced representations can empower these systems to better understand user preferences and item characteristics, leading to more accurate recommendations even with limited data.
literature_themes.limitations: The cluster lacks comprehensive empirical evaluations across diverse datasets and real-world scenarios. Additionally, the scalability of LLMs in practical applications and their computational costs remain unaddressed. There is also a need for clearer methodologies on how to effectively combine LLMs with existing recommendation algorithms.
literature_themes.gap_relevance: This cluster highlights the potential of LLMs in addressing the challenges faced by few-shot recommender systems, thereby identifying a significant research gap in the application of advanced language models in recommendation contexts. It opens avenues for further exploration into hybrid models and their effectiveness in various domains.

summary: The retrieved literature highlights significant safety concerns in large language models (LLMs), particularly in multilingual contexts, emphasizing the need for improved safety assessments and interpretability. Studies reveal that LLMs often produce unsafe responses for non-English queries, necessitating enhanced safety measures and frameworks. Additionally, the integration of LLMs into few-shot recommender systems shows promise for improving performance, though gaps remain in empirical evaluations and methodologies. Overall, the literature underscores the importance of interpretable internal representations to enhance safety and controllability in AI applications.
scholarly_positioning: Existing research on large language models (LLMs) has predominantly focused on safety assessments in specific languages, revealing significant vulnerabilities, particularly in multilingual contexts. However, these studies often lack comprehensive evaluations and fail to address the interpretability of LLMs, which is crucial for trust in sensitive applications like healthcare. Furthermore, while the integration of LLMs into few-shot recommender systems shows potential, the methodologies remain underexplored, limiting practical applicability. This proposed research aims to bridge these gaps by developing interpretable internal representations that enhance both safety and controllability across diverse languages and applications, thereby contributing to the broader discourse on AI safety and ethical deployment.
research_scope: This empirical study will focus on the multilingual safety of large language models (LLMs) by evaluating their performance across 10 languages, particularly targeting non-English queries. The study will develop and apply the XSafety benchmark to assess safety issues in 5 widely-used LLMs, with a specific emphasis on their interpretability in generating safe responses. The evaluation period will span 6 months, during which the models will be tested against a control group of traditional language models. Primary outcomes will include the frequency and types of unsafe responses generated, while secondary outcomes will assess the interpretability of the models' internal representations in relation to safety. This research aims to enhance safety and controllability in LLMs, particularly in sensitive applications like healthcare and education.
gap: Investigate the effectiveness of interpretable internal representations in enhancing safety across underrepresented languages in large language models, focusing on the development of multilingual safety benchmarks and their applicability in real-world scenarios.
question: How do interpretable internal representations in large language models enhance safety outcomes in generating responses for non-English queries compared to traditional language models across 10 different languages?
theoretical_mechanism: The proposed research posits that interpretable internal representations in large language models (LLMs) serve as the independent variable influencing safety outcomes in response generation. The mechanism operates through enhanced transparency (mediator), which allows users to understand and trust the model's decision-making process. This understanding leads to improved user engagement and oversight (intermediate behavior), ultimately resulting in a reduction of unsafe responses (dependent variable). The theoretical framework is grounded in interpretability theory, suggesting that clearer internal representations facilitate better safety assessments. The causal chain follows: interpretable representations -> enhanced transparency -> improved user engagement -> reduced unsafe responses. Key assumptions requiring empirical validation include the premise that increased interpretability directly correlates with user trust and that this trust influences the safety of generated responses.
hypothesis: Interpretable internal representations in large language models will significantly reduce the frequency of unsafe responses for non-English queries compared to traditional language models across 10 different languages.

novelty_contribution: The theoretical novelty lies in establishing a causal framework that links interpretable internal representations to safety outcomes in LLMs, thereby advancing interpretability theory by demonstrating its impact on user trust and engagement. Methodologically, the development of the XSafety benchmark for multilingual safety assessment introduces a novel evaluation design that systematically compares LLMs across ten languages, addressing a significant gap in existing literature. Practically, this research translates theoretical insights into actionable metrics for interpretability and safety, enhancing the deployment of LLMs in sensitive applications such as healthcare and education. This contribution goes beyond mere application of AI by providing a structured approach to understanding and improving the safety of LLMs through interpretable representations, ultimately fostering user trust and reducing unsafe outputs.

proposal: This research proposal aims to investigate the role of interpretable internal representations in enhancing safety outcomes for large language models (LLMs) when generating responses to non-English queries across 10 languages, specifically targeting underrepresented languages to address significant gaps in multilingual safety assessments highlighted in existing literature. The study will develop the XSafety benchmark to evaluate 5 widely-used LLMs, focusing on their interpretability and the frequency of unsafe responses compared to traditional models, thereby addressing the unresolved tension between safety and performance in multilingual contexts. The research question is: How do interpretable internal representations in LLMs enhance safety outcomes in generating responses for non-English queries compared to traditional language models across 10 different languages? The theoretical mechanism posits that interpretable representations (independent variable) enhance transparency (mediator), leading to improved user engagement (intermediate behavior) and ultimately reducing unsafe responses (dependent variable). The falsifiable hypothesis is that interpretable internal representations will significantly decrease unsafe response frequency for non-English queries compared to traditional models. Constructs will be operationalized using model interpretability metrics (measured through output analysis), user feedback (via surveys), engagement metrics (time spent and interactions), and safety incident logs (documenting unsafe outputs). Methodologically, the study will employ a mixed-methods approach, integrating quantitative evaluations of model outputs with qualitative user studies to assess transparency and engagement, while controlling for confounding variables such as user familiarity and cultural context. The baseline models will be clearly justified, and metrics for interpretability and safety will be validated against established standards. Expected contributions include advancing interpretability theory by establishing a causal link to safety outcomes, introducing the XSafety benchmark as a novel evaluation tool, and providing actionable insights for deploying LLMs in sensitive applications. Key limitations include potential biases in model outputs, challenges in accurately assessing safety across diverse languages, and the inability to establish causation beyond the proposed framework, which will be addressed through comprehensive risk analysis and mitigation strategies.
